rejected.title: Skill, biomechanics and energy together
card: A skill is learned through practice and feedback. Biomechanics looks at how the body moves, using ideas such as force, balance and levers. Energy systems and fitness supply the fuel and capacity for the movement.
These three parts depend on each other. A well-learned skill with poor technique wastes force. Good technique that cannot be repeated when tired breaks down.

Fatigue is a common link. It can come from fuel running low, a build-up of by-products such as hydrogen ions (H+), or the body overheating. As muscles tire, movement becomes less accurate and technique can change.
To improve performance, a coach looks at all three. Skill practice can be done in a game-like, tiring setting, and fitness training can be matched to the movements of the sport.
rejected.remember: Performance depends on skill, technique and energy working together, so improving one can mean checking the others.

a.q: Late in a match, a netballer's passes become less accurate and her footwork changes. Which explanation best links the three parts?
opts: Fatigue has reduced her control and changed her technique
Her skill has been unlearned since the start of the match
Her technique has improved because she is moving less
Her fitness plays no part, as accuracy comes from skill
a.why: As muscles tire, movement becomes less accurate and technique can change, which matches what happens to her passes and footwork. Skill is not unlearned during a single match, so the idea that she has lost the skill is the tempting wrong answer.
a.clue: What happens to movement when muscles tire?

b.q: Sam is a swimmer whose stroke technique is sound, but his stroke length shortens in the last 50 m of a 200 m race. Which plan best links skill, technique and energy?
opts: Practise his stroke when tired and train to delay fatigue
Train to delay fatigue, with stroke drills done when fresh
Rebuild his stroke when fresh and keep fitness the same
Add fitness work and drop his technique sessions for now
b.why: His technique is fine when fresh but breaks down when tired, so he needs both fitness work to delay fatigue and stroke practice in a tiring setting. Delaying fatigue while drilling only when fresh is tempting, but it never trains his technique to hold up under fatigue.
b.clue: His technique is fine early in the race.

opts: Fatigue from low energy supply has disrupted her technique
Her skill has been unlearned since the start of the match
Her biomechanics have improved because she is moving less
Her energy systems have stopped, so skill no longer matters

b.q: Sam is a swimmer whose stroke technique is sound, but his stroke length shortens in the last 50 m of a 200 m race. Which plan best fits the idea of linking skill, technique and energy?
opts: Practise technique while fatigued and train to delay fatigue
Only rewrite his stroke, as technique is the sole problem
Only add fitness work, as skill practice no longer helps
Rest more before races and leave his training unchanged
b.why: His technique is fine when fresh but breaks down when tired, so both fatigue and technique under fatigue need work. Changing only the stroke or only fitness ignores the link, which is the tempting choice.
b.clue: His technique is fine early in the race.

a.best: Fatigue from low energy supply has disrupted her technique

b.best: Practise technique while fatigued and train to delay fatigue

problems.detail: The card says fatigue happens 'when the energy supply runs low', as if fuel running out were the only cause. The VCE Study Design also teaches build-up of metabolic by-products (such as H+ ions) and thermoregulatory fatigue. Year 12 students could take away an incomplete idea of fatigue.

A 200 m swim lasts about 2 minutes. Fatigue in the last 50 m comes mainly from metabolic by-products building up during anaerobic glycolysis, not from energy supply running low. Read with the card, the question reinforces the oversimplified cause.

Two wrong options start with 'Only', and the last is plainly unhelpful. The right option is the only balanced, two-part plan, so a student can pick it by spotting the absolute words without knowing the idea.
